title: Hepatocyte senescence in metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).
Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
summary: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.

title: Deciphering auditory neuroprogenitor stemness for large-scale neuronal screening
summary: Sensorineural hearing loss can arise from damage to sensory hair cells, auditory neurons or their synaptic connections, with auditory neuropathy and cochlear synaptopathy highlighting the importance of neural integrity for hearing. The mammalian cochlea has limited capacity to regenerate lost auditory neurons. Understanding the molecular programs that sustain cochlear progenitor expansion and neurogenic competence could support neuronal regeneration and provide renewable models for auditory drug discovery. We previously established that WNT activation combined with dual SMAD inhibition (CHIR-DS) supports scalable expansion and neuronal differentiation of mouse auditory neuroprogenitors (ANPGs). Here, we characterize the transcriptional, chromatin and metabolic changes associated with the induced state. RNA-seq and ATAC-seq identified reduced Id1 and Id2 expression and increased accessibility at proneural basic helix-loop-helix motifs, alongside transcriptional enrichment of translation, mTOR and glucose-metabolism programs. Compared with growth-factor controls, CHIR-DS-treated ANPGs showed slight increase in glycolysis at early passage. However, after long-term expansion, both glycolysis and mitochondrial respiration were markedly enhanced. Human fetal ANPGs also responded to CHIR-DS with increased sphere growth and retained neural differentiation capacity, providing proof of concept beyond the mouse system. Finally, neurons derived from stemness-induced ANPGs (siANs) supported a 384-well reporter assay and a 2,560-compound pilot screen that nominated candidate neurite-outgrowth enhancers. Together, these findings validate the pathway basis of ANPG stemness induction, characterize the resulting molecular and metabolic state, and demonstrate human feasibility and a neuronal screening application.

title: VPS34 regulation in pulmonary arterial vascular smooth muscle cells in pulmonary hypertension
summary: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is characterized by the hyperproliferative phenotype of pulmonary arterial smooth muscle cells (PAVSMCs) and extensive extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling. Vacuolar protein sorting 34 (VPS34), a Class III Phosphatidylinositol-3 Kinase (PI3K), regulates cell proliferation, but its specific function in pulmonary vascular remodeling remains poorly understood. We aim to determine the role of VPS34 activation and regulation in PAVSMC proliferation, matrix deposition, and the progression of PAH. First, we found a marked decrease in the inhibitory phosphorylation of VPS34 at Ser164 (P-S164-VPS34), indicative of constitutive VPS34 activation, in remodeled pulmonary arteries (PAs) from human PAH patients and male mice exposed to Sugen/Hypoxia (SuHx). In human PAH PAVSMCs, siRNA-mediated knockdown of VPS34 or pharmacological inhibition via the selective inhibitor SAR405 significantly blunted cell proliferation and reduced the production of fibronectin, a major component of the remodeled ECM. Mechanistically, we found that Akt activation in PAH PAVSMCs promotes VPS34 activation; Protein Phosphatase 1 Catalytic Subunit Alpha is a potential effector in VPS34 activation; and active VPS34 led to the activation of the mTOR/S6 signaling pathway with tuberous sclerosis complex 2 downregulation. Finally, in vivo treatment with SAR405 attenuated right ventricular systolic pressure, right ventricular hypertrophy, and pulmonary vascular remodeling in SuHx mice, while concurrently decreasing vascular fibronectin deposition. Our study demonstrates that VPS34 activation, driven by an Akt-mediated loss of the inhibitory P-S164, is crucial in PAVSMC proliferation and fibrotic vascular remodeling in PAH. Targeting the VPS34 axis represents a promising anti-remodeling therapeutic strategy for the treatment of PAH. Keywords: Pulmonary arterial hypertension, vacuolar protein sorting 34, pulmonary vascular remodeling, pulmonary arterial vascular smooth muscle

title: Single-cell variant landscape of the human mitochondrial genome reveals cell type-specific functions and disease mechanisms
summary: Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) heteroplasmy is a significant source of cellular genetic diversity and can cause disease yet its distribution and functional importance across different human cell types are poorly understood. Here we present scMOCHA (Single-Cell Mitochondrial Omics for Cellular Heteroplasmy Analysis), a scalable computational framework that resolves highconfidence, single-cell resolution mtDNA heteroplasmy directly from standard single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data. Using this tool to interrogate publicly available scRNA-seq datasets from human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) and bone marrow (BM) uncovered the single-cell landscape of mtDNA single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) and heteroplasmy across ages in human hematopoietic cell types. PBMCs and BM share many inherited homoplasmic and highly heteroplasmic SNVs, whereas somatic SNVs are tissue- and cell type-specific and distributed across the mtDNA genome, suggesting that they arise largely stochastically. mtDNA replication error is a dominant force shaping homoplasmic variants, while oxidative stress potentially drives a significant portion of heteroplasmic and somatic mutations. Importantly, we discover previously unknown cell type-specific and human disease-associated mtDNA SNVs. By coupling mtDNA genotypes with matched single-cell nuclear transcriptomes and structural modeling, we uncover potential molecular mechanisms by which disease-associated mtDNA SNVs impact cellular processes such as inflammation and contribute to disease. Together, these findings define the single-cell variant landscape of the human mitochondrial genome and reveal previously unrecognized lineage- and disease-associated patterns of mtDNA variation in the human hematopoietic system.
